title: Newcastle United owners PIF open to selling minority stake to help fund stadium plans
content:
Newcastle United’s owners are open to selling a minority stake in the club in order to help fund significant infrastructure projects, including a potential replacement for St James’ Park and a purpose-built training ground.

While people familiar with the matter have told The Athletic that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) retain a long-term commitment to Newcastle, the club they bought from Mike Ashley for £305million in 2021, they are willing to dilute their current 85 per cent shareholding and have been approached by possible investors. The British Reuben family own the other 15 per cent of Newcastle.

David Hopkinson, Newcastle’s chief executive, has been pushing to end the sense of stasis regarding the club’s stadium plans and training facilities, both of which have become a source of frustration. St James’ is routinely sold-out but is in need of refurbishment, while Eddie Howe’s first-team squad continue to train in an environment which is more adequate than elite in spite of ongoing improvements.

While a final decision on whether to build a new ground or expand their iconic home is yet to be taken, The Athletic has long reported that senior figures at Newcastle have expressed internally that the preference would be to move.

Both options would be complicated and expensive and although the club have commissioned detailed concepts and designs for staying and going, material progress has been limited and slow, not helped by frequent changes in the leadership structure at the club. Hopkinson intends to change this.

While PIF was never going to pay for a new stadium outright — Newcastle have always been viewed as a long-term investment intended to bring them an eventual profit — any project of that sort would require a notable injection of equity as well as outside financing.

The belief at Newcastle is that PIF selling a minority percentage of the club could kickstart that process and that there are institutional and personal investors willing to pay their way into a business which has largely shown itself to be recession-proof. Internally at Newcastle, there is a view that the club could eventually be worth in the region of £5billion ($6.7bn). Discussions with outside parties, which have not been initiated by PIF, remain at a formative stage.

It comes at a moment when PIF has signalled the end of their funding of LIV Golf, which has so far cost them in the region of £3.7bn ($5bn), and withdrawn from other investments outside Saudi Arabia, sporting or otherwise. That, in turn, has led to suggestions that PIF will seek to sell Newcastle outright, but this has been denied by senior figures at the club.

Hopkinson has stated that the club’s ambition is to be “in the debate about being the top club in the world” by 2030 and there is an acceptance that in order for that to happen, Newcastle must make serious headway on where they will be playing long-term.

In the meantime, they are close to announcing improvements to their hospitality suites at St James’, as well as to their stadium lighting and to the Newcastle Women team’s training facilities at Cochrane Park.

Analysis by George Caulkin

Something needs to give, something needs to happen, someone needs to unpick the logjam.

Newcastle have talked like a big club since their Saudi-led takeover five years ago. On the pitch, Eddie Howe and his players have done their bit but the club have not quite acted like it, certainly in the biggest terms.

Money has been spent on new players (sometimes). St James’ Park has been spruced up. A training ground which Amanda Staveley, the driving force behind the club’s purchase and formerly a co-owner, described as “absolutely appalling”, is now fit for purpose.

But this not an elite environment, not for players and not for supporters who, year on year, have been asked to swallow ticket price increases.

Developments regarding a new stadium, a redeveloped St James’, or a training ground have been glacial. There have been plans and grand designs and video presentations and spikes of engagement, but then very little has materially happened.

From PIF’s perspective, there would be pushback to this argument. Huge decisions which will affect the club for decades should not be rushed to meet clamour. They must be costed and thought-through. They must be right. And, in any case, they would say there has been movement, whether in sourcing a site for a training ground or with the purchase of land around St James’, which The Athletic has written about here.

But this stuff matters. It matters to those fans who cannot get in to see Newcastle play — robbing the club of much-needed revenue — and it matters to Howe, who cannot tell his players they are being given everything they crave, from wages on a level with their Premier League rivals to world-class facilities.

In turn, this has led to a narrative that PIF are reluctant investors or absentee landlords, that they are either uninterested or seeking a way out. While this has always been denied, there has been little in the way of hard evidence.

To compete regularly at the highest level, Newcastle need to find a way forward. They need energy, vigour and activism. Somebody needs to press the button.
